chapter_title: Managing Swap Space and File System Attributes
chapter_summary:
Swap space is a crucial component of memory management in Linux. It is a dedicated area on a hard disk that the operating system uses when the amount of physical RAM (Random Access Memory) is full. When the system runs low on RAM, it moves inactive pages of memory from RAM to swap space, freeing up RAM for more active processes. This process is called "swapping." While swap space can prevent out-of-memory errors and improve system stability under heavy load, it's significantly slower than RAM, so excessive swapping can degrade system performance. Modern systems with ample RAM might not rely heavily on swap, but it's still a recommended practice to configure some swap space, typically as a partition or a file. The general recommendation for swap size varies, but a common guideline is 1x to 2x the amount of RAM, especially for systems with less than 4GB of RAM, or a fixed size (e.g., 4GB) for systems with more RAM.

You can configure swap space in two primary ways: as a dedicated swap partition or as a swap file. A **swap partition** is a regular disk partition specifically designated for swap. To create one, you would first partition a disk (e.g., using `gdisk` or `fdisk`) and set its partition type to Linux swap (type `82` for MBR, `8200` for GPT). Once the partition is created (e.g., `/dev/sdb2`), you initialize it as swap space using `sudo mkswap /dev/sdb2`. After initialization, you activate it with `sudo swapon /dev/sdb2`. To check the current swap usage, you can use `free -h` or `swapon -s`. To deactivate swap, use `sudo swapoff /dev/sdb2`. For persistence across reboots, you must add an entry to `/etc/fstab`: `UUID=<UUID_OF_SWAP_PARTITION> none swap defaults 0 0`. Using the UUID is again recommended for stability.

Alternatively, you can use a **swap file**, which is a regular file on an existing filesystem that is used as swap space. This is more flexible as it doesn't require repartitioning. To create a swap file, first allocate space using `dd` or `fallocate`. For example, to create a 2GB swap file: `sudo fallocate -l 2G /swapfile`. Ensure the file has appropriate permissions to prevent unauthorized access: `sudo chmod 600 /swapfile`. Then, initialize it as swap: `sudo mkswap /swapfile`. Finally, activate it: `sudo swapon /swapfile`. To make it persistent, add an entry to `/etc/fstab`: `/swapfile none swap defaults 0 0`. Using a swap file can be slightly less performant than a swap partition due to filesystem overhead, but the difference is often negligible on modern systems. When removing swap space, always `swapoff` first, then remove the `/etc/fstab` entry, and finally delete the partition or file. Forgetting to `swapoff` before deleting a swap file can lead to errors.

Beyond basic filesystem management, Linux also offers advanced file attributes that can enhance security or data integrity. These attributes are managed using the `chattr` (change attributes) and `lsattr` (list attributes) commands. Unlike standard file permissions (read, write, execute), which control who can access a file, attributes control what can be done to a file by *any* user, including root. The most commonly used attributes are `i` (immutable) and `a` (append-only). When a file has the **immutable attribute (`i`)** set, it cannot be modified, deleted, renamed, or linked, even by the root user. This provides a strong layer of protection against accidental or malicious changes. To set it: `sudo chattr +i /path/to/important_file`. To remove it: `sudo chattr -i /path/to/important_file`. Attempting to modify or delete an immutable file will result in a "Permission denied" error, even as root.

The **append-only attribute (`a`)** allows a file to be opened for writing only in append mode. This means new data can be added to the end of the file, but existing data cannot be overwritten or deleted. This is particularly useful for log files where you want to ensure the integrity of historical data. To set it: `sudo chattr +a /path/to/log_file`. To remove it: `sudo chattr -a /path/to/log_file`. You can view the attributes of a file using `lsattr /path/to/file`. For example, `lsattr /etc/passwd` might show no special attributes, while `lsattr /path/to/important_file` would show `----i--------e-- /path/to/important_file` if the immutable attribute is set. These attributes are a powerful tool for system hardening, but they should be used judiciously. Misapplying them can make system maintenance difficult, as even root cannot easily modify an immutable file without first removing the attribute. Always understand the implications before applying `chattr` attributes.

screens.title: Managing Swap Space and File System Attributes
screens.subtitle: How Linux uses disk as virtual memory, and how special file attributes protect critical data

narration.text: In this lesson you'll learn two practical system-administration skills that help stability and security. First, we explore swap space: what it is, why the kernel moves inactive memory pages to disk, and the two ways you can provide swap — a dedicated swap partition or a swap file. You will see the exact commands used to create, enable, and make swap persistent across reboots. Second, we introduce file attributes managed by chattr and lsattr. These attributes, like immutable and append-only, add a layer of protection beyond normal file permissions. I will show how to apply them, why root is affected by them, and what common mistakes to avoid. Throughout, you will get concrete terminal examples that mirror a RHEL VM workflow: creating a 1GB swap file, verifying with free -h, adding the fstab entry, and protecting a configuration file with +i. By the end you'll know when to add swap, how to avoid errors such as forgetting to initialize or secure a swap file, and how to use chattr attributes safely to harden files. Consider how these controls change your recovery options and maintenance steps.

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Swap prevents out-of-memory failures and file attributes like immutable provide strong, low-level protection for critical files. Together they improve system resilience and hardening.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of these lessons you will confidently manage swap and file attributes on a RHEL system. Objective one focuses on understanding swap space purpose and when swapping helps system stability. You will be able to explain the performance trade-off between R A M and disk-based virtual memory. Objective two covers creating and enabling swap partitions and swap files. You will practice the sequence: allocate, secure, initialize, and activate. Objective three is about persistence: adding correct entries to /etc/fstab using UUIDs for partitions or exact paths for files, and testing with mount -a. Objective four introduces file attributes. You will learn how chattr and lsattr behave, how immutable and append-only affect root, and when these attributes are useful for hardening. Each objective includes a small mnemonic to help you recall the steps during labs. These skills reduce outage risk and protect critical configuration from accidental change. Consider a situation where a low-memory server suddenly needs more virtual memory, and a compliance requirement mandates tamper-evidence for logs; these objectives map directly to solving those problems.

keyIdea.text: Understand swap trade-offs, run the exact terminal sequence safely, make swap persistent, and use chattr attributes for integrity and protection.

screens.title: What is Swap Space?
screens.subtitle: Definition, role in memory management, and when it helps

narration.text: Swap space is disk-based virtual memory that the kernel uses when physical R A M is exhausted or otherwise constrained. Concretely, the kernel identifies inactive memory pages and moves them from R A M to swap to free up memory for active processes. This prevents out-of-memory failures and allows systems to continue operating under heavy load. However, swap is much slower than R A M because disk access latency is orders of magnitude higher, so heavy swapping, often called thrashing, degrades performance. Modern systems with abundant R A M may use swap sparingly, but a small amount of configured swap remains a practical safeguard. A typical guideline is one to two times R A M for very small systems, or a fixed moderate size like four gigabytes on larger machines, but those numbers depend on workload and available R A M. An important misconception is to treat swap as a substitute for insufficient R A M; it is an emergency buffer, not a direct replacement. Swap also enables hibernation on some systems, but that use has its own requirements. When deciding how much swap to provide, consider workload memory patterns, recovery needs, and how often the system touches disk-backed pages. In labs you will observe this behavior by filling memory and watching free -h or swapon -s to see pages moved to swap. Reflect on whether swap will hide memory leaks or only mask symptoms temporarily.

keyIdea.title: Swap is a safety net
keyIdea.text: Swap gives the kernel space to move inactive pages and avoid crashes, but it is slow and not a substitute for sufficient RAM.

content.html:
Core Concept

Swap space defined

Swap is disk space the kernel uses as virtual memory to hold inactive pages. It prevents out-of-memory errors but is slower than RAM.

Key points
  • Swap stores inactive pages when RAM is low.
  • It improves stability but can slow performance if overused.
  • Common checks: free -h and swapon -s.
  • Not a substitute for proper capacity planning.
Key Takeaway

Swap protects against memory exhaustion but is slower than RAM. Use it as a buffer, not as a replacement for RAM.

Analogy: Emergency overflow

Think of RAM as your desk and swap as a filing cabinet. When the desk is full, you move inactive papers to the cabinet. You can keep working, but accessing moved papers takes longer.

Common misconception

Some think increasing swap replaces low RAM. In reality, swap masks the symptom and can hide memory leaks. Plan RAM first, add swap for safety.

Check your understanding
When to use swap
When to upgrade RAM

screens.title: How Swapping Works
screens.subtitle: The kernel's steps for moving pages between RAM and disk

narration.text: Swapping is an internal kernel process with a few distinct steps you should understand. First, the kernel tracks page activity and marks pages as active or inactive. When free R A M falls below thresholds, the kernel selects inactive pages as candidates to move. Second, selected pages are written to swap space — either a swap partition or a pre-initialized swap file — freeing physical R A M. Third, the process that needs the page will later trigger a page-in: the kernel reads the page back into R A M from swap when required. Each of these steps adds latency. A common misconception is that swap always improves performance; in fact, swapping can make interactive tasks sluggish when disk input and output is contended. Another important point is that using a swap file on a fragmented or busy filesystem may be slightly slower than a dedicated swap partition, but modern filesystems and storage make this difference often negligible. In practice you can control swapping behaviour via swappiness settings, but the core concept here is the page lifecycle: mark inactive, write to swap, free R A M, and reload when accessed. In a lab, this becomes visible by running memory-intensive tasks and watching free -h change, or noting a rise in swap usage shown by swapon -s. Consider testing on a non-production VM so swapping won’t impact critical services.

keyIdea.title: Page lifecycle
keyIdea.text: Inactive pages are written to swap to free RAM, and later read back when accessed, which adds latency.

content.html:
Process Flow

Swapping steps

  1. Kernel marks pages active or inactive based on access patterns.
  2. When RAM is low, kernel selects inactive pages as swap candidates.
  3. Selected pages are written to swap space, freeing physical RAM.
  4. When the page is needed later, it is read back into RAM (page-in).
Why latency matters

Disk-backed pages take longer to access. If the system constantly swaps, interactive performance and throughput suffer.

Concrete example

On a small VM with 1GB RAM, launching a memory-heavy process can trigger the kernel to move idle pages to swap. free -h will show swap usage rise while available memory increases. When the heavy process touches swapped pages, you'll notice I/O waits and slower response times.

Common mistake

Assuming swap eliminates the need for more RAM. Swap is a buffer. If workloads require frequent access to swapped pages, plan to add RAM instead.

Key Takeaway

Swapping trades speed for stability. Use it to avoid crashes, not as a primary memory solution.

screens.title: Create a Swap Partition
screens.subtitle: Partition, initialize, enable, and verify swap usage

narration.text: A swap partition is a disk partition formatted specifically for swap. The workflow is: partition the disk, set the partition type to swap, initialize with mkswap, enable with swapon, then verify. Partition tools such as fdisk, gdisk, or parted let you create a new partition and choose the Linux swap type. After creating the partition — for example /dev/sdb2 — run sudo mkswap /dev/sdb2 to initialize it. Then enable it immediately using sudo swapon /dev/sdb2. Verify with free -h or swapon -s. For persistence, obtain the partition's UUID with blkid or lsblk -f, and add a line to /etc/fstab using that UUID: UUID= none swap defaults 0 0. A common omission is forgetting to run mkswap before adding an fstab entry; without initialization the system cannot use the partition as swap. Another pitfall is adding the partition device path to fstab instead of the UUID; device names can change across boots. In labs, create the partition on a non-production disk, initialize, enable, then confirm swap is active. If you later need to remove it, run sudo swapoff /dev/sdb2 before deleting the partition to avoid errors and data issues.

keyIdea.title: Partition workflow
keyIdea.text: Create, initialize with mkswap, enable with swapon, and persist using a UUID entry in /etc/fstab.

content.html:
Process

Swap partition steps

  1. Create a partition and set type to Linux swap (MBR type 82 or GPT 8200).
  2. Initialize the partition: sudo mkswap /dev/sdb2.
  3. Activate: sudo swapon /dev/sdb2.
  4. Verify: free -h and swapon -s.
  5. Persist: add UUID=... none swap defaults 0 0 to /etc/fstab.
Pitfall

Do not add the partition to fstab before running mkswap. Initialization is required for the kernel to recognize swap format.

Terminal walkthrough
# After partitioning and finding /dev/sdb2
sudo mkswap /dev/sdb2
sudo swapon /dev/sdb2
# Verify
free -h
swapon -s
# Get UUID and add to fstab
sudo blkid /dev/sdb2
# In /etc/fstab
# UUID=1111-2222-3333-4444 none swap defaults 0 0
Use blkid to find a stable UUID. Testing with mount -a after editing fstab is a safe way to validate the entry without rebooting.

screens.title: Create a Swap File
screens.subtitle: Allocate a file, secure permissions, initialize, enable, and persist

narration.text: A swap file is a regular file used as swap on an existing filesystem. It avoids repartitioning and is flexible for changing sizes. The sequence is precise: first allocate the file with fallocate or dd. For example sudo fallocate -l 1G /swapfile creates a one gigabyte file. Next, restrict access to root by running sudo chmod 600 /swapfile. This step prevents unauthorized reading of memory contents that may be written to the file. Then initialize the file as swap with sudo mkswap /swapfile and activate it with sudo swapon /swapfile. Verify with free -h. To make it persistent, add /swapfile none swap defaults 0 0 to /etc/fstab. A common error is to add the fstab entry before chmod and mkswap; without proper permissions or initialization the swap will not activate at boot. When removing a swap file always sudo swapoff /swapfile first, then remove the fstab entry, and then delete the file. Forgetting to swapoff before deleting will produce errors. In practice, swap files are slightly slower than swap partitions in some setups, but on modern storage they are often sufficient and much easier to manage. In the next block you will see the exact commands used in the hands-on activity for a 1GB swap file and the safety checks to perform.

keyIdea.title: Swap file sequence
keyIdea.text: Allocate, chmod 600, mkswap, swapon, verify, then persist in /etc/fstab. Always swapoff before removal.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough

Commands to create a 1GB swap file

# 1. allocate
sudo fallocate -l 1G /swapfile
# 2. secure permissions
sudo chmod 600 /swapfile
# 3. initialize
sudo mkswap /swapfile
# 4. enable
sudo swapon /swapfile
# 5. verify
free -h
swapon -s
# 6. persist (add this line to /etc/fstab)
# /swapfile none swap defaults 0 0
Keep the file on a filesystem with enough free space. If fallocate is unavailable, dd can be used but is slower to allocate space.
Safety checklist
  • Use chmod 600 to restrict access before initializing.
  • Run mkswap to format the file for swap use.
  • Enable with swapon and verify with free -h.
  • To remove, run swapoff, remove fstab entry, then delete file.
Example fstab line
/swapfile none swap defaults 0 0

screens.title: Swap File vs Swap Partition
screens.subtitle: Trade-offs and when to choose each

narration.text: Choosing between a swap partition and a swap file depends on flexibility and performance concerns. A swap partition is a dedicated disk area reserved for swap. Historically it offered slightly better performance because the kernel could access a contiguous block on disk without filesystem overhead. A swap file, by contrast, is a regular file inside an existing filesystem and is much more flexible: you can resize it or add one without repartitioning. On modern systems, the performance difference is often negligible, especially with SSDs. Key operational differences are: partitions require partitioning tools and careful device management, while files are created and managed with ordinary filesystem commands. For persistence, partitions are best referenced by UUID in /etc/fstab. For swap files, use the absolute path. A critical operational pitfall is forgetting to run mkswap and chmod on a swap file before adding it to fstab; doing so will leave an invalid entry and swap won't activate. Another important point is that swap files may be subject to filesystem-level features like compression or snapshots; ensure your filesystem semantics are compatible with using a swap file. In practice, for lab and short-term scaling, swap files are often preferred. For long-lived, high-performance systems where every bit of input and output matters, consider a swap partition.

keyIdea.title: Choose by need
keyIdea.text: Use swap files for flexibility and partitions for dedicated, potentially marginally better performance; ensure correct initialization and persistence steps for both.

content.html:
Comparison

Swap Partition

  • Dedicated partition formatted with mkswap.
  • Referenced in fstab by UUID for stability.
  • Historically slightly faster, especially on spinning disks.
  • Requires repartitioning to change size.
Comparison

Swap File

  • Created as a regular file with fallocate or dd.
  • Flexible size and easy to add or remove.
  • Requires chmod 600 and mkswap before use.
  • May interact with filesystem features; test compatibility.
Decision guide
Temporary scaling → swap file
Stable performance → partition
Always initialize and secure first

screens.title: Monitor and Verify Swap
screens.subtitle: Commands and example outputs to check swap status

narration.text: Monitoring swap usage is essential after enabling it so you can confirm activation and observe how much it is used. The simplest command is free -h, which shows total, used, and available memory and swap in human-readable units. Another useful command is swapon -s, which lists active swap devices and files. You can also inspect /proc/swaps for the same information. In a lab you will run these commands before and after enabling swap to see the change. Example output for free -h will show a Swap line with size and used columns. A common oversight is expecting enormous swap use; modest systems often show small or zero swap unless memory pressure exists. Use these commands to tell whether your swap entry in /etc/fstab was effective after a reboot or after mount -a. If swapon -s does not show your entry, check that mkswap was run and that the path or UUID in fstab is correct. Below is a sample sequence and expected outputs you can compare against in the lab. Monitor and Verify Swap means use free -h, swapon -s, and /proc/swaps to confirm swap activation and usage; mismatches usually mean initialization or fstab errors.. In practical terms, commands and example outputs to check swap status. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Verification commands
keyIdea.text: Use free -h, swapon -s, and /proc/swaps to confirm swap activation and usage; mismatches usually mean initialization or fstab errors.

content.html:
Commands
# Show memory and swap
free -h
# List active swap devices/files
swapon -s
# Check kernel swap table
cat /proc/swaps
Run these before and after enabling swap to verify the change. If nothing appears, confirm mkswap and fstab entries.
Example outputs
# free -h (sample)
              total        used        free      shared  buff/cache   available
Mem:           1.0G        700M         50M         10M        250M        200M
Swap:          1.0G        128M        872M

# swapon -s (sample)
Filename                Type        Size    Used    Priority
/swapfile               file        1048572 131072  -2
These samples show a 1GB swapfile with 128MB used. Use them as references when you test on your VM.

screens.title: Safely Remove Swap
screens.subtitle: Deactivate swap, remove fstab entry, and clean up files or partitions

narration.text: Removing swap must be done carefully to avoid disrupting running processes. The safe sequence starts with deactivation: run sudo swapoff /path_or_device to remove the swap area from use. This moves data back into R A M where possible and frees the kernel from using the swap. After swapoff completes, remove the corresponding line from /etc/fstab so it does not re-enable at boot. If the swap was a file, delete the file only after swapoff. If it was a partition, use your partitioning tool to delete or repurpose it. A common error is deleting a swap file without running swapoff first. That causes kernel errors and leaves the system referencing a non-existent backing store. Another pitfall is assuming swapoff is instantaneous; on busy systems it may take time as pages are repatriated to R A M. If you cannot free the swap because R A M is insufficient, consider shutting down nonessential processes or scheduling a maintenance window. Always verify that swap is inactive with swapon -s and free -h. After cleanup, confirm system stability under expected loads before leaving the change in production.

keyIdea.title: Safe removal steps
keyIdea.text: Always swapoff first, update /etc/fstab, then delete the file or partition. Verify with swapon -s and free -h.

content.html:
Process

Removal sequence

  1. Deactivate: sudo swapoff /swapfile or sudo swapoff /dev/sdb2.
  2. Edit /etc/fstab and remove the swap entry.
  3. Delete the swap file or remove the partition definition.
  4. Verify no swap is active and system runs stable.
If swapoff fails because RAM is low, schedule a maintenance window or stop services to free memory first.
Commands
# Deactivate swap
sudo swapoff /swapfile
# Remove from fstab (edit with sudo)
# Then delete file
sudo rm /swapfile
# Verify
free -h
swapon -s
Always confirm swap is gone before removing backing storage. Deleting an active swap store causes kernel errors.

screens.title: File Attributes with chattr and lsattr
screens.subtitle: What attributes do and how they differ from permissions

narration.text: File attributes controlled by chattr and viewed with lsattr add a layer of behavior control beyond standard permissions. While read, write, and execute bits govern who can access a file, attributes control what can be done to the file by any user, including root. The two attributes you'll use most are immutable (i) and append-only (a). When a file is immutable, it cannot be modified, deleted, renamed, or linked, even by root, until the immutable flag is removed. This is useful for protecting critical configuration files. When a file is append-only, new data can be appended but existing data cannot be altered or removed. Log files are a common use case for append-only. To view attributes run lsattr /path/to/file. To set an attribute run sudo chattr +i or sudo chattr +a. To remove one use chattr -i or chattr -a. A misconception to avoid is thinking attributes replace backups or audit controls. They improve hardening, but you must still maintain backups and ensure you can remove attributes when maintenance is required. Another important operational note is to remember that certain filesystems may not support attributes in the same way. Use attributes judiciously and document them so future administrators understand why a file is locked.

keyIdea.title: Attributes vs permissions
keyIdea.text: chattr attributes control file behavior at a lower level than permissions and affect all users including root until removed.

content.html:
Definition

What chattr and lsattr do

Attributes modify how the filesystem treats a file. They are orthogonal to UNIX permissions and can prevent modification even by root.

Common attributes
  • i — immutable: cannot be modified or deleted.
  • a — append-only: can only be opened for append.
Key Takeaway

Attributes are powerful protections. Use them to harden critical files but document and test removal procedures before applying in production.

Commands — view and change
# Show attributes
lsattr /path/to/file
# Make immutable
sudo chattr +i /path/to/file
# Remove immutable
sudo chattr -i /path/to/file
# Make append-only
sudo chattr +a /path/to/logfile
# Remove append-only
sudo chattr -a /path/to/logfile
Confirm attributes with lsattr. If an attribute blocks maintenance, remove it first with chattr -i or -a.

screens.title: Immutable Attribute (+i) — Hands-on Demo
screens.subtitle: Apply +i, observe failures, and restore editability

narration.text: The immutable attribute is a strong safety mechanism. In a demo you create a dummy critical file, write a line, then apply chattr +i and attempt modifications that will fail. For example create /etc/my_critical_config. conf containing configuration data. Initially appending a line should succeed: sudo bash -c 'echo "New line" >> /etc/my_critical_config. conf'. After applying sudo chattr +i /etc/my_critical_config. conf, attempts to append or delete produce permission denied errors, even for root. This behavior shows why attributes are useful to prevent accidental or malicious changes. To restore editability, run sudo chattr -i /etc/my_critical_config. conf and then modify or remove the file as needed. A common misconception is that immutable files are locked forever; they are reversible, but you must remember how to remove the attribute. Also document which files are immutable to avoid surprise maintenance delays. The sample hands-on script below follows the exact sequence you will use in the lab. Observe lsattr output before and after to confirm the i flag appears and disappears. keyIdea.text: chattr +i prevents modification and deletion until you explicitly remove the attribute with chattr -i.

content.html:
Terminal Demo
# Create a dummy config
sudo bash -c 'echo "This is critical config data." > /etc/my_critical_config.conf'
# Show it works
sudo bash -c 'echo "New line" >> /etc/my_critical_config.conf'
cat /etc/my_critical_config.conf
# Make immutable
sudo chattr +i /etc/my_critical_config.conf
# Confirm attribute
lsattr /etc/my_critical_config.conf
# Attempt to modify (will fail)
sudo bash -c 'echo "Another new line" >> /etc/my_critical_config.conf' 2>&1 | grep "Permission denied"
# Attempt to delete (will fail)
sudo rm /etc/my_critical_config.conf 2>&1 | grep "Permission denied"
# Remove immutable
sudo chattr -i /etc/my_critical_config.conf
lsattr /etc/my_critical_config.conf
Note the permission denied lines after applying +i. Removing the attribute restores normal operations.
Key observations
  • lsattr shows an i flag when immutable is set.
  • Even root receives permission denied until the attribute is removed.
  • Document immutable files to avoid blocking maintenance.
Pro Tip

Apply +i to a controlled set of config files and keep a playbook for attribute removal during emergency maintenance.

screens.title: Append-only Attribute (+a) and Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Use cases for +a, combined usage, and operational cautions

narration.text: The append-only attribute makes a file writable only in append mode. This is commonly used for log files where preserving every historical entry matters. When +a is set, processes can add new lines but cannot overwrite or remove previous data. This preserves audit records and reduces the risk of tampering. To set it, run sudo chattr +a /var/log/example. log and confirm with lsattr. Removing it requires chattr -a. In some environments administrators apply both +a for logs and +i for small, critical configuration files. A practical caution is that append-only files may complicate log rotation. Ensure your rotation tooling can handle append-only files, or temporarily remove the attribute during rotation and reapply it. Another operational consideration is that attributes affect root as well; if a scripted maintenance needs to rewrite a file, remove the attribute first. Always document attributes and include attribute changes in change control. Finally, remember attributes are not a replacement for backups or centralized logging. They complement those tools by adding a low-level safeguard against accidental or unauthorized edits. Definition & Use

Append-only (+a)

Append-only allows only adding data to the end of a file. This prevents modification of historical entries. It is ideal for audit logs and append-only ledgers.

Example command
sudo chattr +a /var/log/audit/audit.log
Operational notes
  • Plan for log rotation: remove attribute, rotate, then reapply.
  • Document attribute changes in change control processes.
  • Attributes affect root; have documented procedures to remove them when needed.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the essential ideas to retain. First, swap space is disk-based virtual memory used when R A M is low. It improves stability but is slower than R A M, so use it as a buffer. Second, there are two ways to provide swap: a swap partition and a swap file. Both require initialization with mkswap and activation with swapon; swap files also require secure permissions. Third, make swap persistent by adding correct entries to /etc/fstab, preferring UUIDs for partitions. Fourth, chattr and lsattr let you set file attributes such as immutable (+i) and append-only (+a) that control file behavior at a lower level than permissions. These attributes affect all users, including root, until removed. Use attributes judiciously and always document their application. Finally, monitoring and safe removal procedures are critical: verify with free -h and swapon -s, and always swapoff before deleting a swap file or partition. Keep these checks and procedures in your regular system administration playbook.

keyIdea.text: Swap = safety buffer; initialize and secure before enabling. chattr attributes add strong protections but require careful maintenance planning.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Commands & Practices
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for daily administration

narration.text: Keep three practical reminders front of mind as you apply these skills. First, always allocate, secure, and initialize a swap file before enabling it. The exact commands are fallocate or dd, chmod 600, and mkswap, followed by swapon. Second, persist swap correctly in /etc/fstab and prefer UUIDs for partitions. Test with mount -a to ensure the entry is valid before rebooting. Third, use chattr attributes for protection but plan for maintenance: immutable and append-only affect root and can block scripted changes. Document attribute use and include temporary removal in rotation procedures. These habits reduce surprises during maintenance and ensure safer operations in production environments.
